title: Rabbi Chanina son of Rabbi Abbahu
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.
copyright: English translation and editorial notes © 2026 Joshua Waxman. All rights reserved.
paragraphs: In Jerusalem Talmud Pesachim 3:7 it is related that his father sent him to study in Tiberias. They came and told him that his son was occupied with burying the dead. He sent to him: “Are there no graves in Caesarea, that I sent you to Tiberias?” He received from his father, as in Kiddushin 33b: “[Rabbi] Chizkiyah said: Rabbi Chanina son of Rabbi Abbahu told me that Rabbi Abbahu said that Rabbi Avdimi of Haifa said: When a sage passes by, one stands before him within four cubits.” So it is in Bikkurim 3:5, and there it reads explicitly Rabbi Chizkiyah. At the end of Ketubot, chapter 4: Rabbi Chananyah son of Rabbi Abbahu, and some say it in the name of Rabbi Abbahu: Caesarea follows Judea. In Yevamot 4:11 he said: “Father had a case, and he sent and asked Rabbi Chiyya [bar Abba], Rabbi Yose (Assi) and Rabbi Ami.”

He served as a judge in his city, as implied in Yevamot, chapter 2, end of halakhah 4: a case came before Rabbi Chanina son of Rabbi Abbahu; he said, “Let them marry in a place where they are not known.”

His words we find in Berakhot 7:3, where he said, “It is written ‘in assemblies’”; and in Taanit 1:1 he said: “In the book of Rabbi Meir they found ‘the burden of Dumah — the burden of Domi.’” Of those who speak in his name we find Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yose (the Amora), as in Eichah Rabbah 3:6, where they said: “Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yose in the name of Rabbi Chananya son of Rabbi Abbahu: An incident with a woman in Caesarea who brought her son to a baker to teach him the craft. He said to her: Let him stay with me for five years, and I will teach him five hundred kinds of [baking with] wheat.” In Kohelet Rabbah the words “son of Rabbi Yose” are missing. Seder HaDorot argues and says that this Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yose is the son of Rabbi Yose ben Chalafta, the Tanna; if so, this Rabbi Chananyah son of Rabbi Abbahu would be early. Hyman objects, with respect, that Seder HaDorot did not recognize that in the Jerusalem Talmud Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yose is a late Amora. The source of the story is cited in Nedarim 3b, slightly differently.
Rabbi Berekhyah in his name: Midrash Tehillim 119:4.
Rabbi Chizkiyah in his name: Bikkurim 3:5.
Rabbi Yose (son of Rabbi Bun) in his name: Yevamot 4:11.

notes.text: The supplied ביעור remains genuinely unclear; p002 held instead of inventing the town Ya’ur. חכם עובד is read as the passing sage, עובר, supported by returned Davidson Kiddushin33b. משא דומי remains Domi, also the saved Guggenheimer Taanit1:1 reading; Rome was an unmarked draft substitution, although that paragraph subsequently discusses Rome. Nedarimג: remains3b. Hyman’s Elazar barYose chronology and name variants remain attributed.

The supplied חתנא in the Seder HaDorot discussion is read contextually as התנא, “the Tanna,” in the contrast with a late Amora. Its literal letters remain source data rather than evidence for a new son-in-law relationship; no printed-letter check is claimed. “Stay with me for five years” preserves the baker’s training arrangement and its five-hundred figure.

Hyman’s printed entry (vol. II, p. 478) reads בעירו, “in his city,” where the supplied transcription has ביעור. Jerusalem Talmud Yevamot 2:4:9 records the marriage ruling without naming the city where he judged.

The print and Kiddushin 33b both read עובר, “passes by.” Jerusalem Talmud Bikkurim 3:3:9 gives a parallel with a variant spelling of the Haifa sage’s name. At Jerusalem Talmud Ketubot 4:14:2, Caesarea follows Judean practice in a matter concerning the marriage contract. This accounts for the printed כיהודה where the supplied transcription reads ביהודה.

Eichah Rabbah 3:6 names Elazar son of Rabbi Yose for the wheat episode. The consulted Kohelet Rabbah 1:8:2 gives Elazar without that patronymic in the wheat episode, then tells a separate story about eggs. Hyman’s print reads התנא, “the Tanna,” where the transcription has חתנא. The printed Nedarim reference reads נ:, 50b, beside the supplied ג:, 3b. The proposed parallel remains Hyman’s citation.

The Hebrew of Jerusalem Talmud Taanit 1:1 reads Domi. The accompanying commentary proposes reading it as Rome. In the consulted Yevamot 4:11, Rabbi Yose raises a question before Chanina, and the next discussion quotes Yose son of Rabbi Bun in the name of Rabbi Acha. The list of attributions follows Hyman’s account.
